clean_story:
Group influence. Silent persuasion.

The term social pressure describes the way people in a group push others to act, think, or feel like them, without asking directly. It’s like a river current—you don’t see it, but it pulls you along unless you swim against it.

In school, if everyone starts wearing a certain brand of shoes, the unspoken rule makes others want to do the same. In workplaces, if colleagues always stay late, new employees may feel they must too, even if no one says so. Studies show that in groups of three or more, individuals conform to the majority opinion over 30 percent of the time, even when that opinion is clearly wrong. The mechanism is simple: humans are wired to belong. Rejection once meant danger, so the brain rewards fitting in with dopamine, the same chemical tied to food or laughter.

Social pressure isn’t always negative. It encourages recycling, voting, or helping neighbors during a storm. But it also fuels bullying, risky trends, or staying silent when speaking up matters most. The line between unity and blind conformity is thin.

Three related subjects are peer influence, groupthink and behavioral norms.
